narrative:
The model predicted a 63% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking in the third year of law school was the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Standing in the second decile is well below the average of accepted students (around the sixth decile), signaling that your performance placed you near the bottom of your class. Your first-year ranking had a smaller but still noticeable effect in the same direction; again, a second-decile placement is far below the typical sixth-decile level of admitted applicants.

Your undergraduate GPA worked in the opposite direction, modestly lowering the predicted risk of failure. At 3.10 it sits only slightly under the 3.23 average of accepted students, so the model saw this as a mild positive.

Taken together, the two weak class rankings outweighed the decent undergraduate GPA and produced an overall outlook of likely bar exam failure.

What you should do next is focus on strengthening your academic performance and consider retaking the LSAT. Improving your class standing in future years and raising your test score would directly address the factors that most hurt your application. Many students successfully reapply after targeted improvement in these areas.
